facts.title: Born From Electricity
facts.text: Sodium was first isolated in 1807 by the English chemist Humphry Davy, who passed an electric current through molten sodium hydroxide (caustic soda). He watched tiny silvery globules of pure metal form at the negative electrode. This made sodium one of the first elements ever obtained by electrolysis, a technique still used to produce it industrially today.

facts.title: Why The Symbol Is Na
facts.text: The English name 'sodium' comes from 'soda', the old word for sodium carbonate compounds. Its two-letter symbol Na, however, comes from the Latin 'natrium', which traces back to the ancient Egyptian 'natron', a naturally occurring salt mixture used to dry and preserve mummies. So the symbol on the periodic table is a direct echo of ancient embalming practice.

facts.title: A Metal You Can Cut
facts.text: Pure sodium is so soft that you can slice it with an ordinary knife, revealing a bright silvery surface that instantly dulls to gray as it reacts with air. It is also remarkably light, with a density of about 0.97 grams per cubic centimetre, which is less than water, so a piece of sodium would float, if it didn't react so violently with the water first.

facts.title: It Bursts Into Flame On Water
facts.text: Drop sodium into water and it reacts immediately, producing sodium hydroxide and hydrogen gas while releasing so much heat that the hydrogen often ignites. The reaction can fizz, dart across the surface, and even explode. This is why sodium is stored under kerosene or mineral oil, sealed away from both air and moisture.

facts.title: The Color Of Street Lights
facts.text: When sodium is heated or electrified, it glows with an intense yellow-orange light at two close wavelengths near 589 nanometres, known as the sodium D-lines. This is why classic low-pressure sodium street lamps cast that distinctive amber glow. Astronomers prize these lamps because their single color is easy to filter out, reducing light pollution in telescope images.

facts.title: Half Of Every Salt Crystal
facts.text: The salt on your dinner table is sodium chloride, and roughly 39 percent of its mass is sodium. In each crystal, sodium and chloride ions lock together in a perfectly repeating cubic lattice, each sodium surrounded by six chlorides and vice versa. This orderly arrangement is why salt grains naturally form tiny cube shapes.

facts.title: Your Nerves Run On Sodium
facts.text: Sodium is an essential electrolyte, and your body uses gradients of sodium ions to fire every nerve impulse and heartbeat. Cells spend enormous energy running 'sodium-potassium pumps' that push sodium out and pull potassium in. When a nerve fires, sodium ions rush back inward, creating the electrical signal that lets you think, feel, and move.

facts.title: Sixth Most Abundant On Earth
facts.text: Sodium is the sixth most abundant element in Earth's crust, making up about 2.3 percent of it by mass. It is also the most abundant dissolved metal ion in seawater, which is why the oceans taste salty. Because sodium reacts so readily, it is never found as a free metal in nature, only locked into compounds.

facts.title: Coolant Inside Nuclear Reactors
facts.text: Liquid sodium is used as a coolant in some advanced 'fast' nuclear reactors because it conducts heat extremely well and stays liquid over a wide temperature range, from about 98 to 883 degrees Celsius. Unlike water, it doesn't slow down neutrons much, which suits these reactor designs. The catch is that it must be handled with great care, since it reacts fiercely with air and water.

facts.title: A Tail On A Comet And The Moon
facts.text: Spacecraft and telescopes have detected sodium atoms forming a faint, glowing tail streaming off comets, pushed away by sunlight. The Moon, too, has an ultra-thin atmosphere containing sodium, knocked loose from its surface by sunlight and meteorite impacts. This sodium glow is so distinctive that scientists use it to study these airless worlds from afar.
